newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro-MPs urge Finland, Greece to back ban on mines.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs urge Finland, Greece to back ban on mines.

text.p: The European Parliament on Thursday put pressure on Finland and Greece to join other European Union governments in supporting a worldwide ban on landmines, which kill or maim three people every minute.
The first treaty to ban the use, production, stockpiling and export of landmines is due to be signed by over 100 countries in Ottawa in December.

Finland and Greece are the only members of the 15-nation EU bloc which did not sign a declaration in Brussels last month agreeing to the ban, which has so far won the support of 95 countries worldwide.
"It is a matter of regret that two members of the Union do not currently feel able to subscribe to the total ban," European Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan told the EU assembly.

Euro-MPs later adopted a resolution urging all EU nations to sign the Brussels Declaration and take part "in good faith" in the next round of negotiations on the ban, due to be held in Oslo in September.
They must also take action to stop the illegal trade in landmines, the EU assembly said, urging western governments not to cut funding for mine clearance operations.

Every year, mines kill about 26,000 people, maim thousands more for life and perpetuate hunger and instability in war-torn countries like Afghanistan, Angola and Bosnia by preventing the rural population from returning to their booby-trapped fields.

Apart from Finland and Greece, the most notable absentee from the Brussels Declaration is the United States, which has not signed because it favours separate talks at the United Nations-sponsored Conference on Disarmament in Geneva.

The Geneva talks, which require consensus, are not expected to produce a landmine ban for some years, although a special coordinator on land mines was appointed in June to try and delink the issue from deadlocked talks on nuclear weapons.
